title: Hazel and Waffle's Pancake Picnic
markdown:
The sun came through the trees like a happy spotlight, pink and purple still drying on the sky. Hazel the squirrel twitched her nose. Dew sat on the grass like dropped diamonds. Today smelled like a pancake day.

She zoomed into the oak burrow. “Waffle, wake up, you sleepyhead.”

Waffle the puppy tumbled from his bed with a thump, floppy ears and all. “Pancakes?” His tail made a golden blur.

“The very best kind. Golden, fluffy, piled like a tower. And we are taking them on a picnic.”

Hazel packed extra-syrupy maple in an acorn bottle and a checkered blanket that still smelled faintly of last week’s crumbs. Waffle nudged the biggest flattest stone he could find, then a second stone when the first proved too lumpy. A picnic table, if you believed in stone tables, which they did. They scampered past the root that always tried to trip Waffle, and Waffle tripped anyway, and they laughed, and they reached their secret spot by the babbling brook. Birds practised a merry tune, got the chorus wrong, and tried again. The sun felt like a warm hug that had remembered their names.

Hazel counted the pancakes as she set them down: one, two, three, four, a small fifth for luck. Gold circles still steaming. A thread of maple threatened the edge of the top one; she caught it with a claw. Waffle offered a small bark of approval and sat on his own tail by mistake.

Then a shadow swooped. Another. Another.

Caw. Caw. Caw. A gang of hungry crows landed nearby, beady eyes fixed on breakfast. “Mine,” said a bossy one, puffing like a feathered king. “No, mine,” said a bolder hopper.

“Oh, fiddle-faddle,” yelped Waffle. “They want our pancakes.”

Hazel zipped up the nearest oak and watched the grabby beaks. “We have to protect the stack.” Waffle barked and blocked the path with his bouncy body. The crows only grew braver. One darted. Hazel’s mind did a nutty little click.

She saw bright red berries by the shady bushes. “Waffle. Distract them. Lots of happy silly barks.”

He understood at once. He leaped and spun, the silliest wiggly dance in the meadow. “Look at me. Dancing doggy.” He chased his tail with tremendous gusto, then switched to a hop that was mostly ears. The crows tilted their heads, puzzled by the wobbly show. One almost laughed, if crows do that.

In that second Hazel streaked down, grabbed a pawful of shiny berries, and dashed to the clearing’s edge. Juice stained her paws red. “Look. Big round yummy berries.”

Crows love sparkle almost as much as breakfast. For a flicker they forgot pancakes. Hazel tossed a berry. Plink, near the bushes. They hopped. They gobbled. She tossed another, and another, making a little trail that led away from the blanket like a dotted line in a picture book. Waffle kept the bark-and-wiggle going so their beaks stayed on the feast. When a crow glanced back, Waffle fell over on purpose, which is a kind of art.

“They’re busy.” She pushed the blanket, pancakes and all, under a thick leafy bush. A secret hideaway. Camouflage, if you were a pancake.

The crows, full of juice and still a bit puzzled, looked back. Empty grass where a tower had been. They hopped in a circle, as if the pancakes might be a trick of the light. They ruffled, grumbled, accused one another in crow, and flapped off after easier snacks, leaving only a red stain and a few polite pips.

Waffle leaped. Hazel pulled the stack from the leaves. Still warm. Still smelling like the best idea of the morning. They sat on the checkered cloth. The brook kept talking. A crow, far off, found something that was not breakfast and did not come back.

Hazel poured a careful thread of maple that found every layer. Waffle’s mouth was already full. A crumb travelled to his whisker and stayed, a medal. They did not name the day amazing. They only ate, side by side, while the stone table held the sun and the berries shone, forgotten, where greed had been briefly useful. The brook kept the time. Far above, an oak leaf turned over, as if it, too, had been watching the stack.
